newsitem.title: UK: UK Conservatives soldier on after surprise defeat.
newsitem.headline: UK Conservatives soldier on after surprise defeat.

text.p: British Prime Minister John Major's Conservative government on Tuesday shrugged off a surprise defeat in parliament as a miscount and said it would not change its tactics for the election due by May.

The opposition took advantage of ministers being away at a cabinet brainstorming session at the prime minister's country residence to stage a late-night ambush in the House of Commons on a Monday vote over government education plans.
The opposition Labour Party claimed a knife-edge victory with 273 votes to the government's 272.
But Education Secretary Gillian Shephard told BBC radio's lunchtime news that there had been a miscount and that the opposition victory would be "short-lived".

"We understand that last night the vote was in fact a tie, which under the procedures of the House (of Commons) would have meant that the government didn't lose it, because in those circumstances the Speaker... votes with the government."
Labour said it was not clear what had happened but, under parliamentary rules, the result must stand.
Labour's senior parliamentary business manager, Donald Dewar, said there was a discrepancy between the count of people passing through voting lobbies and the names recorded on a list.

"Whatever happened... it is further evidence of the confusion and chaos which is now surrounding activities in the House of Commons. The reason for that is that the government... is without purpose and simply hanging on and hoping," he said.
"This is a further argument for an early general election."
The government has said it will reinstate the plans -- to let schools which have opted out of local authority control expand -- as the Education Bill goes through parliament.
Health Secretary Stephen Dorrell dismissed suggestions that the government was in trouble and risked being unable to hold on to power until Major's preferred election date of May 1.
"It's the prime minister's job to fix the date, not mine, I'm not going to speculate about that... Nobody's limping along," Dorrell told a BBC radio interviewer on Tuesday.

But Monday night's vote proved how difficult the main opposition Labour Party can make it for the government to keep the upper hand in parliament. Recent opinion polls have shown the Conservatives some 20 points behind Labour.

A breakdown in trust between Labour and the Conservatives has led to the end of cross-party arrangements allowing members of parliament detained elsewhere to miss votes without affecting the result, offering Labour plenty of chances for ambushes.
